text:
Apollo 13: The Long Way Home

By April 1970, Americans had begun to treat trips to the Moon as routine. Two crews had already walked on the lunar surface, and when Apollo 13 lifted off from Florida at 1:13 p.m. Houston time on April 11, none of the three major television networks carried the crew's broadcasts from space live. The commander, Jim Lovell, was flying his fourth mission. With him were Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, and Jack Swigert, who had been in the crew for only three days. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles, and flight surgeons grounded him because he had no immunity. Swigert, his backup, took his seat.

The flight had a small scare on the way up. One of the second stage's five engines shut down more than two minutes early because of violent vibration, and the remaining engines burned longer to make up the difference. After that, things went smoothly. The crew named the command module Odyssey and the lunar module Aquarius. They were bound for the Fra Mauro highlands, where Lovell and Haise planned to collect rocks thought to date from the Moon's early history.

On the evening of April 13, nearly 56 hours into the flight and more than 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew finished a television tour of the spacecraft. Mission Control then asked Swigert to do a routine chore: switch on the fans that stirred the supercold liquid oxygen in the service module's tanks so the gauges would read accurately. He flipped the switch. About a minute and a half later the astronauts heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder.

"Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here," Swigert said. Lovell repeated it a moment later: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first nobody, in space or on the ground, understood how bad it was. Warning lights came on. One of the main electrical circuits lost voltage. The readings from the oxygen tanks made no sense, and engineers in Houston wondered whether their instruments had failed. Then Lovell looked out a window and saw a cloud of gas streaming away from the spacecraft. Oxygen tank number two read empty. Tank number one was losing pressure steadily. The service module's three fuel cells, which combined oxygen and hydrogen to produce electricity and drinking water, needed that oxygen. One by one they were dying.

In Mission Control, flight director Gene Kranz and his team worked through the possibilities and arrived at the only option left. Odyssey would soon have no power apart from a set of batteries that had to be saved for the final hours of the flight, when the command module would carry the crew through Earth's atmosphere. The astronauts would have to move into Aquarius and use it as a lifeboat. With only about 15 minutes of power left in the command module, Lovell and Haise climbed into the lunar module and switched it on, and Swigert shut Odyssey down.

Aquarius had been built to keep two men alive for about two days on the Moon. Now it had to keep three men alive for about four days and get them home. Every resource became a calculation: electricity, water for drinking and for cooling the equipment, oxygen, and the lithium hydroxide that removed the carbon dioxide the crew exhaled.

The landing was off. The immediate problem was getting the spacecraft back to Earth at all. Early in the flight Apollo 13 had left its "free-return" path, a trajectory that would have swung the spacecraft around the Moon and sent it home without further engine burns. The service module's main engine sat right next to the damaged area, and no one trusted it. About five and a half hours after the explosion, the crew fired the lunar module's descent engine, which had been meant to lower Aquarius to the lunar surface, and put the spacecraft back on a path that would loop around the Moon and fall back toward Earth.

On April 14 Apollo 13 swung behind the Moon. Because of the geometry of that path, Lovell, Haise, and Swigert went farther from Earth than any humans before or since, nearly 249,000 miles. Lovell had orbited the Moon on Apollo 8 and had seen this view before, but Haise and Swigert had not, and they took photographs of the surface they would not land on. About two hours after the closest approach, the crew fired the descent engine again in a long burn that sped up the return by roughly ten hours and moved the splashdown point to the Pacific Ocean, where the recovery ships waited.

The new course solved one problem and left several others. Carbon dioxide was building up in the cabin. The lunar module's air scrubbers used round canisters of lithium hydroxide, and there were not enough of them for three men over four days. Odyssey had plenty of spares, but those canisters were square and would not fit the lunar module's system. Engineers in Houston worked out an adapter using only items they knew were on board: plastic bags, cardboard from the flight plan covers, hoses from the spacesuits, and a lot of gray duct tape. They read the instructions to the crew step by step. The astronauts built the device, which became known as the "mailbox," and the carbon dioxide levels began to fall.

The cold was harder to fix. With most systems powered down to save electricity, the spacecraft had very little heat. Temperatures inside fell to around 38 degrees Fahrenheit, and moisture condensed on the walls and instrument panels. The crew limited themselves to a few ounces of water a day so the lunar module's equipment would have enough for cooling. They slept badly, if at all. Haise developed a urinary tract infection and ran a fever. All three lost weight.

Navigation was another concern. To save power the crew had shut down the computer that normally steered the spacecraft, and debris from the explosion floating alongside made it hard to sight stars. When the trajectory drifted and needed a correction, Lovell flew the burn by hand, holding the edge of the Earth steady in a window while Haise and Swigert called out the timing.

Meanwhile, on the ground, Ken Mattingly and a team of engineers worked in simulators to answer a question no one had planned for: how do you restart a command module that has sat cold and dark for days, using only the little power its batteries hold? They wrote a new power-up sequence that stayed within the battery limit, and they found a way to recharge Odyssey's batteries from the lunar module. Swigert copied the long procedure by hand as it was read up to him.

On the morning of April 17 the crew prepared for reentry. They released the service module first, and as it drifted away they saw for the first time what had happened: an entire side panel had been blown off, exposing the damaged interior. Swigert brought Odyssey back to life, and the procedure worked. About an hour before reentry, the astronauts released Aquarius. "Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you," a voice from Mission Control said.

Reentry always caused a radio blackout of several minutes as the heat around the capsule blocked transmissions. This time the silence ran longer than expected, and in Houston the controllers waited without knowing whether the heat shield had been damaged. Then Swigert's voice came through. Television showed three parachutes opening above the Pacific, and at 12:07 p.m. Houston time Odyssey splashed down near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima.

An investigation later traced the explosion to a chain of earlier mistakes. Oxygen tank number two had been dropped a couple of inches at the factory years before. During a test on the launch pad, the tank would not empty normally, and technicians ran its internal heater for hours to boil off the oxygen. A thermostat switch meant to protect the tank had been designed for the spacecraft's 28-volt power, not the 65 volts used on the ground, and it welded shut. Temperatures inside the tank rose high enough to damage the insulation on the wires. When Swigert turned on the fans in flight, a spark ignited it.

NASA redesigned the service module before the next flight. Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, but the crew came home alive, and the mission is often called a "successful failure."
